summary: Stack memory is automatic, fast, and tied to function scope. Heap memory is manual, larger, and lives until you free it. Choosing correctly decides performance and bug surface.

sections.heading: Stack allocation
bullets: Locals and parameters are placed in a frame created on call and destroyed on return.
Allocation is just moving the stack pointer, so it is very fast.
Size is limited (often 8 MB on Linux by default).
Data cannot outlive the function that created it.

sections.heading: Heap allocation
bullets: `malloc`/`calloc`/`realloc` request memory from the allocator; `free` returns it.
Lifetime is whatever you decide, independent of scope.
Much larger than the stack, but allocation has bookkeeping cost.
You must free exactly once and never use it afterward.

sections.heading: Comparison
bullets: Speed: stack is faster; heap pays allocator overhead.
Typical failure: stack overflow vs leaks, dangling pointers, fragmentation.

sections.heading: Pointers connect them
sections.body: A very common pattern is a pointer variable on the stack that refers to a block on the heap. When the function returns the pointer vanishes; if you did not free the block (or hand the pointer on), it leaks.

Each recursive call adds a frame. Missing base cases, or locals like `char big[10*1024*1024]`, exhaust the stack and the process is killed by SIGSEGV. Fix by bounding recursion, iterating, or moving large buffers to the heap.
Repeated allocate/free of different sizes leaves small holes. Total free memory may be large yet no single hole fits a request. Allocators mitigate with size classes and coalescing.
Returning `&local` hands back stack memory that is already invalid. Return a heap pointer, a `static`, or fill a caller-provided buffer.
sections.code:
int *bad(void)  { int x = 1; return &x; }          // dangling
int *good(void) { int *p = malloc(sizeof *p); *p = 1; return p; }

subtopics.title: Heap data structure vs heap memory

sections.body: The 'heap' in priority queues is a tree-shaped data structure. The 'heap' here is the process memory region used for dynamic allocation. They are unrelated.

takeaways: Stack: automatic, fast, scoped, small. Heap: manual, flexible, large, slower.
Never return the address of a local variable.
Every malloc needs exactly one free.
Use the stack by default; use the heap when size or lifetime demands it.
